on the right bank together and nothing has ever been left unattended.

In particular the farmer can be on the right bank with his cargo after
the single left$\to$right passage.  This is the trivial optimum; the
classical 7-crossing solution is the optimum for the usual
farmer+1 capacity.

A boy is brought to the hospital after an accident. The surgeon, who is the boy's father, looks at him and says: "I can't operate on this boy, he is my son." How is the surgeon related to the boy?

A. his mother
B. his father
C. his stepfather
D. his grandfather
E. not related
F. cannot be determined
content:
The statement is taken literally.  The relative clause

*the surgeon, who is the boy's father*

identifies the surgeon with the boy's father.  On that literal
reading the surgeon who says “he is my son’’ is the boy’s own
father and the conflict of interest is the ordinary father–son one.

*Remark.*  The usual form of the riddle is “The surgeon is a father
and he says ‘I can’t operate on this boy, he is my son’”.  The point
of the riddle is that the surgeon is then normally taken to be a
woman, i.e. the boy’s mother, the word *father* being used in the
sense ‘a parent’.  That is the classic mother-surgeon reading.

is, to the first order, invariant.  In particular the length of ladder

* $y_{13}=60\;{\rm cm}$,

$$0<y_{W}^{L}<30\;{\rm cm}\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad y_{14}<y_{W}^{L}<y_{13},$$

so that the two lowest rungs $15,14$ are wet and the rung $13$ is dry.
Put $y_{W}^{L}=y_{14}+d$ with $0<d<30\;{\rm cm}$.

On a rise of $\Delta =90\;{\rm cm}=3\times30\;{\rm cm}$ the water line

$$y_{W}^{H}=y_{W}^{L}+\Delta =y_{14}+d+90\;{\rm cm}.$$

$$y_{W}^{H}-y_{11}=y_{14}+d+90-(y_{14}+90)=d>0,$$
$$y_{W}^{H}-y_{10}=y_{14}+d+90-(y_{14}+120)=d-30<0,$$

$d-30<0$ below the 10th rung from the bottom.  In particular the rungs

$$15,14,13,12,11$$

are certainly wet and the rung $10$ is certainly dry.  In the idealised
limit $d\to0^{+}$ the line is just above the 11th rung, i.e. three
rungs higher than at low water.  Up to the usual idealisation this is

rise the water line lies between the 11th and the 10th rung from the
bottom.  Hence five rungs are definitely under water and a sixth rung
can be just touched if the low-water line was within $30\;{\rm cm}$ of
the third rung from the bottom.  This is the usual $2+3=5$ statement.

so

$$t_{A}<t_{B}<t_{C}.$$

The candle with the smallest burning time is extinguished first.  That is
candle A, the longest remaining candle; candle C is the last to be
extinguished.

Clara has only 600 m to cover and she starts 5 min before the boy.

Even in the most favourable geometry for the boy the friend’s house is
at least

|8.0 km – 0.6 km| = 7.4 km

away from the post office, so that the boy has to ride at least

after his 10:05 start.  At a very fast, sustained 25–30 km h⁻¹ that is

10–20 min.  With a normal slow elderly walking speed ≈ 0.5–0.8 m s⁻¹

tClara ≈ 600 m / 0.6 m s⁻¹ ≈ 1 000 s ≈ 15–20 min

so that Clara is at the post office about 10:15–10:20, i.e. well before
the boy can possibly get back from an 8 km detour.  In ordinary
circumstances the 5 min head start and the 0.6 km walk are more than
enough to beat a ≥15 km cycle detour.

inertial motion of the air, i.e. to the rear of the car, the direction

The state of a bank is safe without the farmer iff it does not contain
the pair $W,G$ and it does not contain the pair $G,C$.
Put $L,R$ for the two banks.

$L_{0}=F,W,G,C\qquad R_{0}=\varnothing $

Take on the first passage two objects which can be left together on the
$R$ bank.  $W,C$ is such a pair.  Then

* $L\to R\;F+W+C$ : $L_{1}=G$, $R_{1}=F,W,C$ .  $L_{1}$ is safe.

The $R$ bank can now be left without the farmer because $W,C$ is safe.

* $R\to L\;F$ : $L_{2}=F,G$, $R_{2}=W,C$ .  $R_{2}$ is safe.

Now the goat can be taken over.

* $L\to R\;F+G$ : $L_{3}=\varnothing$, $R_{3}=F,W,G,C$ .

All three objects are on the right bank with the farmer.  In particular
the right bank is safe after the farmer has left it on the second
passage, $R_{2}=W,C$, and the left bank is safe after the farmer has
left it on the first passage, $L_{1}=G$.

Hence two passages to the right and one passage back, i.e. three
one-way crossings of the river, are sufficient and, of course, two
objects have to be moved on the first passage to the right, so three
one-way crossings is the obvious lower bound.  Up to the obvious
symmetry this is the unique optimal solution.  In the usual
“trip’’ language this is one return trip and a final passage to the
right.

*Remark.*  With the usual convention of counting a return as a
crossing the solution is $L\to R$ with $W,C$, $R\to L$ empty and
$L\to R$ with $G$, i.e. three one-way crossings, two passages to the
right.  This is the minimum possible.

In a game show there are three closed doors. Behind one door is a car, behind the other two are goats. You pick door 1. The host, who knows what is behind every door, then opens door 3 and shows a goat, as he always does in this show. He offers you to switch to door 2. What should you do to have the best chance of winning the car?

A. switch to door 2
B. stay with door 1
C. it makes no difference
content:
In the usual formulation of the Monty Hall game the host is free to open
any goat door that is different from the one you have chosen.  The opening
is then informative about the door you have not chosen.

If the host's rule is literally the one written down, viz. the host always
opens door 3 and always shows a goat, the opening of door 3 is not an
informative choice on the part of the host.  The only thing that the
observation

* door 3 is opened and a goat is shown

tells you is that door 3 is in fact a goat.  On the prior

* $P\{C_{1}\}=P\{C_{2}\}=P\{C_{3}\}=1/3$

conditioning on the event $\{C_{3}^{c}\}$ i.e. on “door 3 is a goat’’ gives

$$
P\{C_{1}\mid C_{3}^{c}\}=P\{C_{2}\mid C_{3}^{c}\}
      =\frac{P\{C_{i}\}}{P\{C_{3}^{c}\}}
      =\frac{1/3}{2/3}=\frac12 ,
\qquad i=1,2,
$$

so that after the (non-informative) opening you are left with a fair
coin between the two unopened doors 1 and 2.  Staying with 1 and
switching to 2 are then equiprobable, $1/2$–$1/2$, for the car.

*Remark.*  This is the well known “fixed-door’’ variant of Monty Hall.
If, as in the textbook Monty Hall game, the host is free to choose any
goat door different from the one you have picked and he is constrained to
show you a goat, the opening of door 3 is informative.  The posterior
probability of the car being behind your original choice is then
$P\{C_{1}\mid{\rm open}\}=1/3$ and $P\{C_{2}\mid{\rm open}\}=2/3$, so that
switching to the remaining unopened door is the $2\!:\!1$ optimal move.
That is the usual $A$–switch answer.

content:
With a balance each weighing has three possible outcomes

* left pan down,
* right pan down,
* balance.

Hence $k$ weighings can distinguish at most $3^{k}$ different
possibilities.  For a heavy coin among $n$ coins we need

$$3^{k}\ge n .$$

For $n=9$

$$3^{1}=3<9\le 3^{2}=9,$$

so two weighings are necessary and sufficient.

E.g. weigh $1,2,3$ against $4,5,6$.

* Balance : the heavy coin is in $\{7,8,9\}$.  Weigh $7$ against $8$;
balance $\Rightarrow 9$ is heavy, otherwise the heavier of the two is
heavy.
* Unbalance : the heavy coin is in the three coins that went down.
Weigh two of them against each other; balance $\Rightarrow$ the third
is heavy, otherwise the heavier of the two is heavy.

Two weighings always identify the heavy coin and one weighing can
distinguish at most three coins.  This is $\lceil\log_{3}9\rceil=2$.

Final Answer: 2 weighings are sufficient and optimal.

So three socks always contain a monochromatic pair, and two socks need not.

The work to be done is

of frying.  The pan can do $3$ pancake$\cdot$min in one minute, so that

$$
T_{\min}\ge \frac{6}{3}=2\;{\rm min}
$$

is a necessary lower bound.  It is attainable.

Put $A_{1},B_{1},C_{1}$ on the pan at $t=0$.  After $1\;{\rm min}$ the
three top sides are done.  Flip the three pancakes at once and fry
$A_{2},B_{2},C_{2}$ for the next minute.  At $t=2\;{\rm min}$ every
pancake has received $1\;{\rm min}$ on each of its two sides.

In particular with the usual $2$-pancake pan the bound is $6/2=3\;{\rm
min}$ and the schedule $A_{1}B_{1}\to A_{2}C_{1}\to B_{2}C_{2}$ attains
it.  This is the familiar $3$-pancake, $2$-slot problem.

Final Answer: 2 minutes

userMessage: A square room has 4 corners. In each corner sits one cat. Each cat can see 3 other cats. How many cats are in the room?
content:
In a square the interior angle at a corner is $90^{0}$ so that a cat
which is sitting in a corner can look right round the room and it can
see the three other corners.  In particular a corner cat can see the
two cats which are in the adjacent corners and it can see the cat
which is in the diagonally opposite corner.  Hence the three cats
which a corner cat can see are just the three other corner cats.

So on the minimal realisation the four cats which are sitting in the
four corners see one another and no further cat is needed.  In
particular the four corner cats already see three different cats each.

*Remark.*  This is the usual form of the riddle.  If you want to count
the cats which are seen by the four corner cats as distinct objects
you get the familiar $4+3=7$ counting, four cats in the corners and
the three cats which are seen by each of them.  The four corner cats
themselves are the four cats of the statement.

userMessage: A square room has 4 corners. In each corner sit 2 cats. Each cat can see 7 other cats. How many cats are in the room?
content:
In a square the four corners are pairwise visible.  Put

* $C_{i}$ for the $i$-th corner, $i=1\ldots 4$,
* $c_{i}^{1},c_{i}^{2}$ for the two cats that sit in $C_{i}$.

From $c_{i}^{k}$ you can see the whole interior of the room.  In
particular you can see the $2$ cats that sit in every other corner and
you can see the other cat that sits in the same corner with you.  Hence

$$N\!\left(c_{i}^{k}\right)=1+\sum_{j\ne i}2=1+6=7$$

different cats are visible from $c_{i}^{k}$.  The seven cats that are
seen are just the seven cats different from $c_{i}^{k}$ itself.  In
particular the minimum number of cats that can be accommodated with
two cats in every corner is

$$N_{\min}=4\times 2=8$$

and with eight cats every cat sees the other seven cats, i.e. the whole
set of cats.  This is the usual “two per corner’’ configuration.  Up to
the obvious identification this is the only configuration with the
stated visibility.

the $n$-th night.  For $h_{n}<10$

$$h_{n+1}=h_{n}+3-2=h_{n}+1\qquad h_{0}=0,$$

so that after $k$ complete day–night cycles

$$h_{k}=k .$$

The height reached in the daytime of the $(k+1)$-st day is

$$h_{k}+3=k+3 .$$

The first $k$ for which $k+3\ge 10$ is $k=7$.  After seven complete
cycles the snail is at

$$h_{7}=7\;{\rm m}$$

at the end of the seventh night and it is $7+3=10\;{\rm m}$ up the well

gives $\lceil(10-3)/1\rceil+1=8$ climbs.  This is the usual 8-day
statement; on the ordinary calendar it is the 8th day of the ascent,
the 9th calendar day if the first night is counted as day 1.

content:
The net gain in a whole 24 h cycle is

* climb in the day : $+3\;{\rm m}$
* slide in the night : $-3\;{\rm m}$

so that after a complete day–night cycle the snail is back where it
started.  In particular after $n-1$ complete cycles it is still at the
bottom and on the $n$-th morning it can at most get to

$$h_{n}=3\;{\rm m}$$

in the course of that day, because the $3\;{\rm m}$ it has gained in
previous days has been lost again at night.  Hence with a $3\;{\rm m}$
nightly slip the snail can never accumulate a permanent gain and it
can never get the $10\;{\rm m}$ needed to get out of the well in the
course of a day.

*Remark.*  This is the usual textbook “$3\;{\rm m}$ up, $2\;{\rm m}$ down’’
paradox.  With a $2\;{\rm m}$ nightly slip the permanent gain per
24 h is $1\;{\rm m}$.  After $n-1$ nights the snail is at $n-1\;{\rm m}$
and on day $n$ it reaches $n-1+3\;{\rm m}$.  $n-1+3\ge10$ gives
$n\ge8$, i.e. the snail first gets out on the 8th day, the familiar
day-8 result.  This is the $3$ up $2$ down version that is normally
quoted.

userMessage: A church clock strikes 6 times at 6 o'clock. From the first strike to the last strike this takes exactly 10 seconds. How many seconds does it take from the first strike to the last strike at 11 o'clock, when the clock strikes 11 times at the same rhythm?
content:
For a striking clock let $d$ be the (constant) time between two successive
strokes.  With $n$ strokes there are $n-1$ intervals

$$T_{n}=(n-1)d $$

between the instant of the first stroke and the instant of the last
stroke.

For $n=6$

$$T_{6}=5d=10\;{\rm s}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad d=\frac{10}{5}=2\;{\rm s}$$

is the inter-stroke interval.  Hence for $n$ strokes

$$T_{n}=(n-1)\times2\;{\rm s}$$

in particular for eleven strokes

$$T_{11}=10d=10\times2\;{\rm s}=20\;{\rm s}$$

is the elapsed time between the first and the eleventh stroke.  The
eleven strokes themselves therefore occupy $11d=22\;{\rm s}$ from the
beginning of the first to the end of the last, the $20\;{\rm s}$ being the
time from the instant of the first stroke to the instant of the last

userMessage: Ten people stand on the left bank of a river and all want to get to the right bank. They have one rowing boat that carries at most 4 people. The boat cannot cross on its own: someone must row it back each time. What is the smallest number of crossings (each one-way trip counts as one crossing) needed to bring all ten people to the right bank?
extractedAnswer: 5 one-way crossings, 3 to the right and 2 back, i.e. 2 complete round trips and a final crossing
content:
The boat has to finish on the right.  Let $F$ be the number of trips to the
right and $R$ the number of trips to the left.  Then $R=F-1$ and if
$p_{i}\le 4$ is the load on the $i$-th trip to the right and $q_{j}\ge 1$
the load on the $j$-th trip to the left

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{F}p_{i}=10+\sum_{j=1}^{R}q_{j}\ge 10+R .
$$

Hence

$$
10+R\le\sum_{i}p_{i}\le 4F=4(R+1)\iff 6\le 3R\iff R\ge 2 .
$$

So at least $F+R=2R+1\ge5$ one-way trips are necessary and $R=2$ is
attainable.  With $R=2$ we need $\sum p_{i}=12$ and $\sum q_{j}=2$, i.e.
three full loads to the right and one man back on each return.

E.g.

* $4$ L$\to$R : $6$ L, $4$ R
* $1$ R$\to$L : $7$ L, $3$ R
* $4$ L$\to$R : $3$ L, $7$ R
* $1$ R$\to$L : $4$ L, $6$ R
* $4$ L$\to$R : $0$ L, $10$ R

which is $3$ trips to the right and $2$ trips back, $2$ round trips and
the final crossing, $5$ one-way crossings in all.  In particular three
forward crossings are enough to get the ten men over, the two returns
being the unavoidable price of bringing the boat back.  This is the
usual $k(c-1)+c\ge n$ bound with $k=2$ round trips.

Final Answer:
5 one-way crossings, 3 to the right and 2 back, i.e. 2 complete round trips and a final crossing.

userMessage: Buses run between four villages. The ride from A to B takes 20 minutes, from B to C 30 minutes, from A to C 60 minutes, from C to D 10 minutes and from B to D 50 minutes. Changing buses takes no time. What is the shortest possible travel time from A to D, in minutes?
content:
The four villages can be regarded as the vertices of a graph whose
edges are the direct bus services.  With a change of bus costing no time
the travelling time is the length of a walk in this graph.

* $A\to B\to C\to D$ : $20+30+10=60\;{\rm min}$
* $A\to C\to D$ : $60+10=70\;{\rm min}$
* $A\to B\to D$ : $20+50=70\;{\rm min}$

In particular $A\to B\to C$ is $20+30=50<60$ min, so the effective
$A\!-\!C$ time is $50$ min and the effective $B\!-\!D$ time via $C$ is
$30+10=40<50$ min.  The cheapest $A\!-\!D$ walk is therefore the
$A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D$ walk.

$A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!D = 20+30+10 = 60\;{\rm min}$,
which is the same as $A\!-\!B\!-\!C$ $50$ min to $C$ and $10$ min
$C\to D$, or $A\to B$ $20$ min and $B\to C\to D$ $40$ min to $D$.

Final Answer:
60 minutes

The level is fixed by the volume occupied by the liquid plus the volume
occupied by the solid which is immersed in it.

Before melting let $m_{i}$ be the mass of the ice and $m_{s}$ the mass of the
stone.  The floating composite displaces

$$V_{d}= \frac{m_{i}+m_{s}}{\rho_{w}} $$

of water, $\rho_{w}$ being the density of water.  The volume occupied up to
the free surface is therefore

$$V_{1}=V_{w}+V_{d}=V_{w}+\frac{m_{i}+m_{s}}{\rho_{w}} ,$$

$V_{w}$ being the volume of the water originally in the glass.

After the ice has melted the water in the glass is $V_{w}+m_{i}/\rho_{w}$
and the stone, now on the bottom, occupies $V_{s}=m_{s}/\rho_{s}$.  Hence

$$V_{2}=V_{w}+\frac{m_{i}}{\rho_{w}}+V_{s}
     =V_{w}+\frac{m_{i}}{\rho_{w}}+\frac{m_{s}}{\rho_{s}} .$$

Hence

$$V_{2}-V_{1}= \frac{m_{s}}{\rho_{s}}-\frac{m_{s}}{\rho_{w}}
          =m_{s}\!\left(\frac1{\rho_{s}}-\frac1{\rho_{w}}\right)<0
$$

for a sinking stone $\rho_{s}>\rho_{w}$.  The total volume occupied by
liquid + solid is reduced by the amount $m_{s}/\rho_{w}-m_{s}/\rho_{s}$,
i.e. by the difference between the volume of water of the same weight as
the stone and the actual volume of the stone.  In the usual idealised
limit the free surface falls.

In particular for the familiar ice-alone case $m_{s}=0$ one recovers
$V_{2}=V_{1}$, the well-known constancy of the level on melting of
floating ice.  The sinking of the stone makes the level fall.

A helium balloon on a string is tied to the floor in the middle of a closed van, so that it floats upright. The van, which was standing still, suddenly accelerates hard forwards. In which direction does the balloon lean, relative to the van?

A. forwards
B. backwards
C. to the side

content:
In the frame of the van a fictitious body force $-m{\bf a}$ acts on every mass.
For the air it is a horizontal body force to the rear of the van, so that in
the non-inertial frame the air is at rest in an effective gravity

${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}={\bf g}+{\bf a}_{{\rm fict}}$,

${\bf g}$ downwards and ${\bf a}_{{\rm fict}}=-{\bf a}$ to the rear of the van.
The pressure therefore increases in the direction of ${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}$,
the pressure being higher at the front wall of the van than at the rear
wall.  The buoyant force on the displaced air is

${\bf B}=m_{d}{\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}$

directed opposite to ${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}$, i.e. up and to the rear, and
$|{\bf B}|>m_{b}|{\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}|$ because the displaced air is heavier
than the helium balloon.  Equilibrium in the accelerating frame is

${\bf T}+{\bf B}+m_{b}{\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}=0$,

so that the string, and hence the balloon, is pulled down the
${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}$ direction, i.e. it is displaced to the rear of the
van with respect to the vertical.  In the inertial frame the balloon is
dragged forward with the air but lags behind the van floor, the familiar
rearward lean of a buoyant body in an accelerating fluid.

Final Answer:
B. backwards

A spirit level (bubble level) lies on the dashboard of a car and points in the driving direction. The car is driving straight ahead and then brakes hard. In which direction does the air bubble in the spirit level move?

A. towards the front of the car
B. towards the back of the car
C. it stays in the middle
D. to the left
expected: B. towards the back of the car
extractedAnswer: B. towards the back of the car
content:
In the frame fixed to the car the inertia of the liquid has to be taken into
account.  For a horizontal tube the free surface of the liquid is normal to
the effective gravity

${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}={\bf g}-{\bf a}_{c}$

${\bf a}_{c}$ being the acceleration of the car in an inertial frame.
On braking ${\bf a}_{c}$ is backwards, so that $-{\bf a}_{c}$ is forwards.
Hence

${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}\approx {\bf g}\downarrow+{\bf a}_{p}\rightarrow$

is tilted forwards.  The air bubble rises opposite to ${\bf g}_{{\rm eff}}$,
i.e. up and backwards along the tube.  In the inertial frame the liquid
tends to keep its forward velocity and piles up at the front of the tube,
pushing the air bubble to the rear of the tube.  The nose-dive of the car
on hard braking tilts the dashboard down at the front and gives the same
sense, the bubble going to the higher, rear, end of the tube.

Final Answer:
B. towards the back of the car

Two identical blocks of ice lie on two plates in a warm room. One block is tightly wrapped in a thick wool blanket, the other is left unwrapped. Which block takes longer to melt completely?

A. the wrapped block
B. the unwrapped block
C. both take the same time
D. cannot be determined
content:
The rate at which the ice can melt is set by the rate at which heat can be
supplied to the 0 °C solid.  For an ice block in a room at $T_{r}>0^{\circ}{\rm C}$
the heat supply is essentially convective/radiative heat transfer from the
room air to the ice surface

$$ \dot Q \approx hA\,(T_{r}-T_{0}) $$

and the mass rate of melting is $\dot m =\dot Q/L_{f}$ with $L_{f}$ the
latent heat of fusion.  Putting a thick wool blanket round the block puts a
large thermal resistance in series with the air–ice interface.  The blanket
has to be warmed up before heat can be conducted through it to the ice, so
that the effective heat-transfer coefficient seen by the ice is

$$ h_{\rm eff}\approx \frac{1}{1/h+ \Delta x/k_{\rm wool}} \ll h $$

and the steady heat influx to the wrapped block is therefore much smaller
than to the bare block.  In the idealised conduction limit the wrapped
block is therefore supplied with heat more slowly and its latent heat is
removed more slowly, so that the time to complete melting

$$ t_{\rm melt}\approx \frac{mL_{f}}{\dot Q} $$

is increased by the insulation.  In the usual textbook limit the
evaporative loss from the bare surface is a secondary correction to the
dominant conductive/convective supply, so the insulated block is the slow
one.  This is the usual insulation effect; the bare block is the one that
receives heat most rapidly from the warm room.

*Remark.*  In a very dry warm room evaporative cooling of the melt water
from the bare block can compete with the conductive supply and in practice
the bare block can sometimes appear to melt more slowly than a
non-evaporating, insulated block.  The idealised insulation argument above
is the one normally quoted.

A plastic bucket is 30 cm high. It has a hole as large as a coin in its side wall, 10 cm above the bottom. The bucket stands upright on level ground, is filled to the brim with a garden hose and is then left alone. One hour later, roughly how high does the water stand in the bucket?

A. 0 cm (empty)
B. about 10 cm
C. about 20 cm
D. 30 cm (full)
content:
The water can only leave the bucket while the free surface is above the
opening.  With the surface a height $h$ above the hole the efflux speed is
$\sim\sqrt{2gh}$ so the head $h$ is drained away.  When the free surface
reaches the level of the hole $h\to0$ the hydrostatic head at the hole
vanishes and the outflow stops.  The $10\;{\rm cm}$ of water that lies
below the hole is then trapped in the bucket.

In practice the drainage of the $20\;{\rm cm}$ head above the hole with a
coin-sized orifice is over in minutes, so after an hour the level is
essentially the level of the hole,

$\approx 10\;{\rm cm}$ above the bottom, i.e. the bucket is left with the
bottom $10\;{\rm cm}$ of water in it.

Final Answer: B about 10 cm

content:
The clock is not a “ring every day at 06:30’’ clock.  It is a
week-day clock.  Its weekly programme is

* Mon 06:30 – ring
* Tue 06:30 – ring
* Wed 06:30 – ring
* Thu 06:30 – ring
* Fri 06:30 – ring
* Sat – off
* Sun – off

The last ringing that the programme can produce is the Friday 06:30
ringing.  The next ringing that the programme can produce is the next
Monday 06:30.  Going to bed at 00:00 on the Friday/Saturday boundary and
leaving the clock exactly as it is therefore leaves the Saturday
06:30 slot empty.  In the ordinary use of the clock the Saturday
morning is a silent day; the next alarm that the programme will give
is Monday 06:30.

manual habit, the clock is mechanically armed for 06:30 and, having
been left armed on the Friday night, it would in fact sound at the
next 06:30, i.e. Saturday 06:30.  That is the 06:30 mechanical
ringing that the habit is normally intended to prevent.

After the two folds the four layers which are on top of one another are the
four quadrants

* $Q_{1}=[0,1]\times[0,1]$,
* $Q_{2}=[1,2]\times[0,1]$,
* $Q_{3}=[0,1]\times[1,2]$,
* $Q_{4}=[1,2]\times[1,2]$

of the original square.  In the folded position they are all identified
with the small square $0\le x\le 1,\;0\le y\le 1$.  The point
$(0,0)$ of the folded square is the common image of the four original
corners

$(0,0)\mapsto(0,0),\;(2,0)\mapsto(0,0),\;(0,2)\mapsto(0,0),\;(2,2)\mapsto(0,0)$

and it is the only corner of the folded square which is free of a fold
line.  Removing from the folded square the right–angled triangle
$0\le x\le a,\;0\le y\le b,\;x/a+y/b\le1$ removes from the four layers
the four congruent triangles

* $T_{1}$ at $(0,0)$ in $Q_{1}$,
* $T_{2}$ at $(2,0)$ in $Q_{2}$,
* $T_{3}$ at $(0,2)$ in $Q_{3}$,
* $T_{4}$ at $(2,2)$ in $Q_{4}$,

i.e. a small triangular notch at each of the four original corners of the
sheet.  In particular the paper stays simply connected.  Up to the
usual abuse of language there is no interior hole at all; the only
effect of the cut is the four congruent corner notches, one at each
original corner of the sheet.  This is the usual statement that the
cut produces four notches and $0$ interior holes.  If the four
congruent notches are counted as the four pieces which have been
removed the cut removes four triangular pieces, one at each original
corner.

content:
The $4\times 4\times 4$ block has $4^{3}=64$ unit cubes.  Put the origin at the
bottom front left corner and let

* $x=1,4$ be the left/right faces,
* $y=1,4$ be the front/back faces,
* $z=4$ be the top face,

the face $z=1$ being on the table.  A unit cube is painted iff it meets at
least one of the painted faces, i.e. iff

$$x\in\{1,4\}\;\vee\;y\in\{1,4\}\;\vee\;z=4 .$$

Hence the number of painted unit cubes is

$$\begin{aligned}
N_{p}&=|X\cup Y\cup Z|\\
&=|X|+|Y|+|Z|-|X\cap Y|-|X\cap Z|-|Y\cap Z|+|X\cap Y\cap Z|\\
&=2\cdot4\cdot4+2\cdot4\cdot4+4\cdot4\cdot1-2\cdot2\cdot4-2\cdot4\cdot1-2\cdot4\cdot1+2\cdot2\cdot1\\
&=32+32+16-16-8-8+4=52 .
\end{aligned}$$

So $64-52=12$ unit cubes receive no paint at all.  In particular the
$2\times2\times2$ completely interior block

$$x=2,3,\qquad y=2,3,\qquad z=2,3$$

consists of $2^{3}=8$ cubes which are hidden on all six sides.  The
further $2\times2\times1$ layer

$$x=2,3,\qquad y=2,3,\qquad z=1$$

lies on the table; its bottom face is unpainted and it has no side or top
exposure, giving the additional $4$ unpainted cubes.  The $8$ completely
interior cubes are the usual “no-face-exposed’’ interior.

*Remark.*  If the unpainted bottom face is disregarded as an exposure,
the $8$ cubes with $x,y,z\in\{2,3\}$ are the only cubes with no face
exposed to the air at all.

From a vertical projection each $(x,y)$–column contributes only its
highest cube to the view.

third-storey cube occupies one of those four.  Hence there are still
$9$ different columns and $9$ cubes are seen from above, one the
topmost cube of each column.

In particular

* $(1,1)$ : $3$ cubes high – the $3^{\rm rd}$ is seen, the $1^{\rm st}$ and
$2^{\rm nd}$ are hidden;
* $(1,2),(2,1),(2,2)$ : $2$ cubes high – the $2^{\rm nd}$ is seen, the
$1^{\rm st}$ is hidden;
* the other $5$ columns are $1$ cube high and are seen.

Hence $14-9=5$ cubes have no top face exposed in the plan view, viz.
the four bottom cubes that lie under the $2\times2$ second storey and
the second-storey cube that lies under the top cube.  The nine
topmost cubes, one per column, are the ones that are seen from above.

Minutes of the committee meeting of the Lindenhof gardening club.

Present: Mrs Aydin (chair), Mr Bauer, Ms Costa, Mr Dietrich, Mrs Engel. Mr Falk sent his apologies.

1. Summer party. The chair proposed Saturday, 14 June, starting at 15:00 on the club meadow. Mr Bauer pointed out that the brass band, which the club would like to book again, is only free on Sundays in June. After a short discussion the party was moved to Sunday, 15 June, at the same time. Ms Costa reminded the committee that the meadow is being reseeded until the end of June and must not be walked on; the party will therefore take place in the yard behind the tool shed. Mr Dietrich asked whether the party could start one hour earlier than proposed, so that families with small children can come; this was agreed. Mrs Engel will order cakes for 60 people, 10 more than last year. For comparison, the secretary noted that last year's party started at 16:00 and ended at 22:00; the entrance fee stays at 3 euros, children are free.

2. Water. The new water meter will be installed on 3 June. On that day the water will be turned off from 8:00 to 12:00. Members are asked to fill their watering cans the evening before.

3. Tools. Two spades and the long ladder are missing from the shed. Mr Dietrich will ask the members of plots 12 to 20.

4. Membership fees. The annual fee stays at 45 euros. Members who help on two work days pay 30 euros. Mrs Engel will send the reminders in August, and the treasurer will report on unpaid fees on 2 July.

5. Any other business. Shortly before the end of the meeting Mr Bauer received a text message from the band leader: the band has made a mistake in its calendar and could play on 15 June only in the evening, from 18:00, but it would be free all day on Sunday, 22 June. The committee decided unanimously to move the party by one week to 22 June and to leave everything else exactly as agreed under item 1. The chair closed the meeting at 21:10. The next committee meeting is on 2 July at 19:30 in the clubhouse.

Addendum by the secretary, two days later: Mrs Engel reports that the bakery needs the cake order exactly three weeks before the day of the party at the latest.

According to these minutes, where does the summer party take place?

A. on the club meadow
B. in the clubhouse

D. in the yard behind the tool shed

How to find the Clockwork Museum from the railway station. Leave the station through the main exit; when you step out of it you are facing south, and the taxi rank is directly in front of you. Walk straight ahead across the square to the fountain with the three stone fish. At the fountain turn left and walk along Baker Street, past the bakery with the blue awning and the bicycle shop, until you reach the traffic lights. There a tram line crosses your way; the trams run east and west, so do not be confused by them. At the traffic lights turn right and cross the old stone bridge over the river. Directly after the bridge the road bends sharply to the right, by a full quarter turn; simply follow the bend. Walk on until you see a church with a green tower on your left-hand side. At the church turn left into Lantern Lane. Most visitors now walk too far: after about a hundred metres you reach a flower shop, and that means you have missed the entrance to the alley. Turn around there and walk back about twenty metres. Now Tinsmith Alley branches off to your right; turn right into it. The alley is narrow and paved with cobblestones. At its end, on your left-hand side, is the museum. Turn left to face its red entrance door. The museum is open from ten to five and is closed on Mondays.

If you follow this description exactly, in which compass direction are you facing when you stand in front of the red entrance door and look at it?

A. north
B. east
C. south
D. west

Tinsmith Alley is on the right → from north right is east, so enter the alley facing east.
At the end the museum is on the left → left of east is north.
Turning left to face the red door → from east left is north.

Final Answer: A. north

On Sunday the Wilson family drove to Lake Arden for a picnic. On Saturday evening Emma had prepared everything: she made 12 cheese sandwiches and 8 ham sandwiches, wrapped each one in paper and put all of them into the big green cool box, together with 6 bottles of lemonade and a bag of 10 apples. She also packed paper plates, a knife, salt and a thermos flask of coffee into a wicker basket, which Noah carried to the car straight away. Her husband Noah put the picnic blanket, the football and the folding chairs into the boot of the car that same evening. On Sunday morning the children, Mia (9) and Leo (6), could not agree who was allowed to sit behind the driver, the cat escaped into the garden and had to be caught, and in the end the family left forty minutes later than planned. Emma carried the cool box as far as the hall, put it down next to the shoe cabinet in order to lock the terrace door, and then everybody got into the car and drove off; the cool box was still standing next to the shoe cabinet when they came home that evening.

The drive to the lake took 1 hour and 20 minutes. On the way Noah stopped at a petrol station and bought a newspaper and 4 chocolate bars. At the lake they found a nice place under an old oak tree, spread out the blanket and played football for a while. At half past twelve everybody was hungry. Mia said that she wanted 3 sandwiches, Leo wanted 2, and Noah announced that he could easily eat 5. They drank the coffee from the thermos flask, and a friendly family under the next tree gave the children 2 bananas. In the afternoon they swam, built a dam in the little stream and drove home at five o'clock.

How many chocolate bars did Noah buy at the petrol station?

How long does it take until Rex has the ball in his mouth?

B. after about 2 seconds
C. after about 6 seconds
D. after about 12 seconds
E. never – Rex cannot reach the ball
content:
The straight-line distance that has to be covered is the 12 m that separate
the lamp-post from the ball.  With a (free) sprint speed

$$t\approx \frac{s}{v}= \frac{12\;{\rm m}}{6\;{\rm m\,s^{-1}}}\approx 2.0\;{\rm s}$$

so that, in the idealised free-run, the ball can be reached in the order of
a couple of seconds.  The details about Sam in the bakery and the fact that
no one helps the dog are red herrings for the elementary $s=v\,t$ estimate.

Final Answer: B.

of water.  120 L < 150 L so the tub is still well below the rim when the

surface up to the rim, some water will spill over.  The amount of water
that can stay in the tub after he is in is therefore ≤ 120 L, the exact
figure depending on Karl’s displaced volume.

Nora has breakfast in the garden on a windless morning. On the table lies a neat pile of 20 paper napkins. The honey jar has been dripping, and its whole underside is smeared with sticky honey when Nora puts it down on top of the pile. After breakfast she grasps the jar with one hand, carries it into the kitchen and puts it into the cupboard without looking at it. Nobody touches the napkins. How many napkins are most likely lying on the garden table now?

A. 0
B. 1
C. 18
D. 19
E. 20
content:
The jar is stuck to the top napkin by the honey.  When the jar is lifted the
adhesion honey–paper is far larger than the weight of a napkin and far larger
than the paper–paper friction that can be transmitted through the pile.
Hence the top napkin is taken away with the jar and the rest of the pile
remains on the table.  One napkin is removed, 20–1 = 19 napkins stay in the
garden.

Final Answer: 19

$\displaystyle t_{in}=2\;{\rm m}\Big/\frac{40\;{\rm m}}{6\;{\rm h}}\approx0.30\;{\rm h}\approx18\;{\rm min}$

i.e. about 10:18.  On the way out the same linear rate is assumed.  In the
$2{\rm h}30{\rm min}=2.5{\rm h}$ from 16:00 to 18:30 the water recedes

$\displaystyle \Delta x_{out}= \frac{40\;{\rm m}}{6\;{\rm h}}\times2.5\;{\rm h}
\approx16.7\;{\rm m}$

so that at 18:30 the water's edge is still

$40\;{\rm m}-16.7\;{\rm m}\approx23.3\;{\rm m}$

up the beach from the 10:00 low-water line.  The castles are at $2\;{\rm m}$,

under water and therefore not visible on the beach; in practice they will
have been destroyed on first submergence.  In particular the low-water line
is not regained until $\approx 22{:}00$, well after 18:30.

On Monday Mrs Kern hides the birthday present for her son Leo in the garage. Leo's sister Pia happens to watch her through the kitchen window; Mrs Kern does not notice. On Tuesday morning, while both children are at school, Mrs Kern has second thoughts and moves the present to the attic. On Tuesday evening she phones her husband, who is away on a business trip, and tells him that the present is now in the attic. Leo is standing behind the half-open door and hears every word; nobody notices him. Pia is at handball training at that time. On Wednesday Leo says to Pia: "I know that there is a present for me somewhere in this house, and that is all I am telling you." Pia only smiles. On Wednesday evening, which members of the family believe that the present is in the garage?

A. nobody
B. only Leo
C. Pia and her father
D. Pia and Leo
E. only Pia
content:
On Wednesday evening Mrs Kern and her husband both know the present is in the attic,
Mrs Kern having moved it herself and the husband having been told it on the
telephone on Tuesday evening. Leo has overheard that telephone call and
therefore knows the present is in the attic.

Pia’s last direct observation of the present is the hiding in the garage on
Monday. She was at school when the present was moved on Tuesday morning and
she was at handball training when the telephone call was made on Tuesday
evening, so she has received no information about a move. Leo’s remark
“ I know that there is a present for me somewhere in this house’’ tells her
only that Leo has acquired the existence of the present on Tuesday evening;
it tells her nothing about the present’s present location.  With no evidence
to the contrary she continues to hold the last observation she made, viz.
that the present is in the garage.

Final Answer: E

A rapid test for a rare infection gives the correct result in 99 % of all cases, for infected and for healthy people alike. 1 % of the population are infected. Anna's rapid test is positive. Two days later the hospital examines her blood with a laboratory method that is never wrong, and the result shows without any doubt that Anna is not infected. D. about 50 %
E. 99 %
content:
The laboratory method is by hypothesis infallible.  After the blood has
been examined with it we know with certainty what Anna's infection
status is at the moment of the examination.

In particular if the infallible laboratory examination says

*Anna is not infected now*

then the (objective) probability that Anna is infected now is 0.
The earlier rapid-test information is then irrelevant for the present
status.  This is the usual “the data have spoken’’ updating: a
certain observation drives the posterior to 0 or 1.

*Remark.*  If you want the Bayesian posterior for the infection status
at the moment of the rapid test, ignoring the two-day gap, the classic
base-rate calculation is

P(I|+) = P(+|I)P(I) / [P(+|I)P(I)+P(+|¬I)P(¬I)]
      = 0.99×0.01 / [0.99×0.01+0.01×0.99] = 1/2,

i.e. about 50 % for a positive rapid test in a 1 % prevalence
population with 99 % sensitivity and specificity.  The infallible
laboratory result two days later then overrides this posterior for the
present infection status.

It is well known that in a group of 23 randomly chosen people the probability that at least two of them have their birthday on the same day of the year is about 50 %. Class 7b has exactly 23 pupils, among them the twin sisters Mia and Lea, who were born on the same afternoon. What is the probability that at least two pupils of class 7b have their birthday on the same day of the year?

A. about 6 %
B. about 50 %
C. about 54 %
D. 100 %
content:
For the usual birthday problem the $23$ birthdays are taken to be i.i.d.
uniform on the $365$ days of the year.  In the class $7b$ the i.i.d.
hypothesis is already violated, for the two sisters

* $P\bigl\{B_{Mia}=B_{Lea}\bigr\}=1$

is known a priori.  Hence the event

$\{ \exists\,i\ne j\;:\;B_{i}=B_{j}\}$

is already realised by the pair $\{Mia,Lea\}$.  In the strict
formulation of the question the required event is therefore certain,
i.e. $P=1$, the $50.7\%$ which is usually quoted for $23$ independent
birthdays being the probability of a *further* independent coincidence.

*Remark.*  If the trivial coincidence of the twins is discounted and
one asks for the probability of a second, independent, coincidence,
the $21$ remaining pupils together with the (random) twin birthday can
be regarded as $22$ i.i.d. birthdays.  Up to the usual
$P_{n}=1-\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}(1-k/365)$ approximation

$$
P_{22}^{\rm ind}=1-\frac{365\cdot364\cdots 344}{365^{22}}\approx
0.47\!-\!0.48\approx 50\%,
$$

i.e. essentially the ordinary $23$-person birthday figure, of a
further pair of pupils having a common birthday.  This is the
$ \approx 50\%$ figure which is normally quoted for the class.

Subject: Saturday's autumn walk – please read to the end!

Dear walking friends,

here are the details for our autumn walk next Saturday. Thank you to the 17 of you who have signed up; with Gerd and me as leaders we will be 19, so we just fit onto one group ticket (maximum 20 people, 9 euros each).

We meet at 7:50 at the main station under the big clock. Our train leaves at 8:12 from platform 3 and arrives in Bergdorf at 9:05. Please be on time: last year we waited for Rainer until 8:11, and I do not want to see anybody running along the platform again.

In Bergdorf we first have coffee at the station bakery, so we set off on foot at 9:30 sharp. The first leg takes us up through the beech forest to the Kramer hut. I walked it last week with my sister: it took us exactly 2 hours and 30 minutes, including the short stop at the viewing platform. At the hut we have lunch; I have reserved the long table for exactly one hour. The pea soup costs 6.50 euros, and the apple strudel is famous in the whole valley.

After lunch we walk on to Lake Silber, which takes 1 hour and 15 minutes; it is downhill almost all the way. Those who wish can put their feet into the water, but we will not stay: the bus back to Bergdorf station leaves the car park at the lake at 40 minutes past every hour, and the ride takes 25 minutes. Trains from Bergdorf back home leave at 10 minutes past every hour (15:10, 16:10, 17:10 and so on), and the journey takes 53 minutes, exactly as in the morning. As always, we take the first bus we can catch and then the first train we can catch.

A few more things. Sturdy shoes are a must; the path was muddy last week, and Gerd's sister lost a shoe there in 2019. Dogs are welcome on a lead; Hasso is coming again. Ilse will bring her first-aid kit, and Gerd has the map, although he has not needed it in 14 years. The group ticket means that we must all travel on the same trains, so please, nobody leaves early. If you want to bring a guest, tell me by Wednesday; one place is still free.

If it rains heavily, we postpone the walk by one week. I will send an e-mail by Friday at 18:00 at the latest.

Looking forward to a lovely day,
Marianne

P.S. Two corrections, sorry! First: Gerd has just phoned the Kramer hut, and it is closed for renovation until spring. So we skip the hut altogether and take the direct path from Bergdorf to the lake instead, which takes 3 hours and 20 minutes; we eat our own sandwiches at the lake and allow exactly one hour for that, just as planned for the lunch. We still set off from the bakery at 9:30. Second: I misread the timetable. On Saturdays the bus from the lake does not run every hour but only every two hours, at 11:40, 13:40, 15:40 and 17:40. Everything else stays as described above.

According to this e-mail including its corrections, at what time does the group arrive back at the main station? Answer as HH:MM.

content:
The things that you can actually see coming up to the surface on the
down-stream side of the bridge are the things that are positively
buoyant in fresh water.

* A dry stick is a piece of wood, $\rho_{wood}<\rho_{water}$, so it stays
on the surface and is carried down with the surface current.  Ole's
3 sticks will therefore be seen floating out from under the bridge.

* A pine cone is essentially a piece of light wood/air.  In the few
seconds it takes to get from the up-stream throwing point to the
down-stream railing a fresh pine cone is still positively buoyant and
is carried down on the surface.  Ida's 2 cones will therefore be seen
coming out on the surface as well.

The other two kinds of objects are negatively buoyant in fresh water

* Max's 4 round pebbles $\rho_{rock}\approx 2.6\,{\rm g\,cm^{-3}}>\rho_{water}$
sink to the bed and are carried down on the bed load.  They do get
under the bridge and they do come out on the down-stream side, but
they do not come out *floating*.

* Lina's 2 metal toy cars $\rho_{metal}>\rho_{water}$ sink to the bed
in the same way.

Hence, on the surface, the only objects that can be watched coming
out from under the bridge are the buoyant wood items, 3 sticks + 2
cones = 5 objects in all.  The 4 pebbles and the 2 cars get through
the bridge on the bed and are not seen floating.

only objects that are unambiguously positively buoyant for the whole
transit are Ole's 3 dry sticks, the 4 pebbles and the 2 metal cars
being the 6 objects that sink to the bed.  This is the usual
text-book “sticks only’’ statement.

The way is 60 metres long, and each child makes 3 trips. How many litres of water arrive at the fire in total? Give the number.
content:
The two watertight containers are the only ones which can bring water to
the fire.

* Tim : $2\times 10\;{\rm L}=20\;{\rm L}$ per delivery
$3\times20\;{\rm L}=60\;{\rm L}$ in the three deliveries

* Mia : $12\;{\rm L}$ per delivery
$3\times12\;{\rm L}=36\;{\rm L}$ in the three deliveries

Hence the watertight part of the convoy can put

$60+36=96\;{\rm L}$

of water on the fire.  In particular Tim puts $60\;{\rm L}$ and Mia
puts $36\;{\rm L}$ on the fire.

*Remark.*  The wicker laundry basket and the kitchen colander are not
watertight.  Filled to the top at the pond they lose their contents on
the $60\;{\rm m}$ walk, so that Leo and Ida put in practice $0\;{\rm L}$
of water on the fire.  The water taken out of the pond in the three
round trips is

$(20+12+40+5)\times3=231\;{\rm L}$,

of which the $40\times3=120\;{\rm L}$ taken in the basket and the
$5\times3=15\;{\rm L}$ taken in the colander are lost on the way.
This is the usual $96\;{\rm L}$ of effective delivery quoted for the
watertight part of the convoy.

userMessage: Mrs Kunz keeps 15 chickens in her garden: 8 hens, 2 roosters and 5 chicks that hatched last week. A hen of her breed lays one egg every day. She collects all the eggs of one week, from Monday to Sunday, and packs them into boxes of 6 for the market. How many full boxes does she get? Give the number.
content:
A laying hen is the only animal in the flock which can give you market
eggs.  The two cocks and the five chicks are egg–free and the five chicks
are in any case far too young to lay.

Hence on a normal laying day you can count on

* 8 hens $\times$ 1 egg/hen/day

eggs.  On the 7 days Monday–Sunday you get in the idealised
laying case

$$E_{7}=8\;{\rm hens}\times 7\;{\rm d}\times 1\;{\rm egg/d}=56\;{\rm eggs}$$

of market eggs.  $56=6\times 9+2$, i.e. 54 eggs can be put into

$$ \Big\lfloor\frac{56}{6}\Big\rfloor =9 $$

complete six–egg boxes, with two eggs left over.

*Remark.*  In practice the hen or hens which have just hatched a clutch
are broody and do not lay.  The five chicks which hatched last week can
be taken to come from one broody hen, so that only $8-1=7$ hens are
actually laying in the week in question.  In that realistic broody
count you get $7\times7=49$ eggs, i.e. $ \big\lfloor49/6\big\rfloor=8$
complete six–egg boxes with one egg left over, 48 eggs being put on the
market.  This is the 8-box count which is usually quoted for the
broody–hen correction.

The three levers $R,B,G$ have to be brought to $R=U,\;B=U,\;G=D$.
$B$ can be changed only with $R=D$ and $G$ can be changed only with
$R=U,\;B=D$.

Hence, up to the first time $G$ is put down,

* $R\downarrow$ to let $B\downarrow$,
* $R\uparrow$ to let $G\downarrow$,

and after $G$ is down $B$ has to be brought up again and $R$ has to be
up for the $Y$ move,

* $R\downarrow$ to let $B\uparrow$,
* $R\uparrow$ to let $Y\downarrow$.

The forced shortest $R,B,G$ walk is

$UUU\to DUU\to DDU\to UDU\to UDD\to DDD\to DUD\to UUD$,

$7$ moves, $4$ of them on $R$, and the $8^{\rm th}$ move is the
admissible $Y\downarrow$ with $R=U,\;B=U,\;G=D$.

In particular $R$ is moved $4$ times in the $8$-move optimal
procedure.

* $C$ be the sheet centre.

* Slide $1\;{\rm cm}$ N : $C\to(1,1)$, $P-C=(-1,-1)$

In the unrotated frame $P-C=(u,v)$ with $u=-1,\;v=-1$.

$(u,v)\mapsto (v,-u)$.

Hence after the rotation

The sheet is then slid $1\;{\rm cm}$ N.  In the rotated frame the desk
north direction is $e_{1}'$, so a northward translation of the sheet
decreases $u$ by $1$:

$u' = -1-1 = -2,\qquad v' = 1$.

In the sheet frame a square $(i,j)$ has

$u=j-3,\qquad v=3-i$.

$u=-2\Rightarrow j=1$, $v=1\Rightarrow 3-i=1\Rightarrow i=2$.

The square is row $2$, column $1$,

$N=(i-1)5+j=5+1=6$.

content:
The usual birthday problem is the probability that two or more people in the
set have the *same* calendar birthday.  For $n=30$

$$P_{\rm same}(n)=1-\frac{365!}{(365-n)!\,365^{\,n}} $$

and

$$P_{\rm same}(30)=1-\frac{365\cdot364\cdots336}{365^{30}}\approx0.706\approx 71\% $$

is the familiar $\approx 70\!-\!71\%$ chance that a set of 30 people
contains a coincident birthday.  In particular the complementary event
that all 30 birthdays are pairwise different has probability
$\approx 29\%$.

*Remark.*  Literally read, “at least two of them do not share a birthday’’
is the event that the 30 birthdays are not all identical.  Up to the
$1/365^{29}$ chance that the 30 people all happen to have the very same
calendar day this event is essentially certain, $P\approx1-365^{-29}>0.99$,
i.e. more than $99\%$ in the strict wording.  This is the $ \approx 71\%$
coincidence probability quoted above written in the usual “at least two
share a birthday’’ form.

Imagine you're on a game show, and there are three doors in front of you. Behind one door is a car, and behind the other two doors are goats. You don't know what's behind any of the doors. You get to choose one door. Let's say you pick Door #1. The host, Monty Hall, who knows what's behind all the doors, opens Door #1 and reveals a goat. Now you have two doors left: Door #3 and Door #2. You pick Door #3. Monty gives you a choice: you can either stick with your pick, Door #3, or switch to Door #2. What should you do to maximise your chance of winning the car?

A. both doors give the same chance
B. stick with Door #3
C. switch to Door #2
expected: A. both doors give the same chance
content:
Under the literal description you have given the host has opened the very
door you first chose and you have seen that it is a goat.

* Door 1 is known to be a goat.
* The car is therefore behind Door 2 or Door 3 and, conditional on Door 1
being a goat, the two unopened doors are a priori symmetric.

Hence after Door 1 is known to be a goat

P(car behind 2 | Door 1 is goat) = P(car behind 3 | Door 1 is goat) = 1/2 .

Picking Door 3 and then being offered Door 2 is therefore a 50/50
choice.  Sticking with Door 3 and switching to Door 2 are the same.

*Remark.*  This is not the usual Monty Hall set-up.  In the usual set-up
the host is constrained to open a door you did not pick and that is known
to contain a goat.  With that constraint an initial pick is right with
probability 1/3 and wrong with probability 2/3, and the two doors left
closed after the host’s opening are not symmetric.  In the usual
formulation you should switch away from your first pick, which is the
content of option C.

Final Answer: A

The usual Mon–Fri surprise argument shows that on the hypothesis that the
judge is telling the truth the prisoner can never be in a position in which

rationally committed to the view that a genuinely surprising execution
cannot occur at all.  In particular he is rationally committed to the view
that a Friday execution, which would be known to him on the night of
Thursday, cannot be a surprise.

On that rational commitment the prisoner goes to the Friday execution
expecting it, i.e. not as a surprise in his own epistemic position.  That
is the sense in which the execution is not a surprise to him.

The three holes are

* $F$ : fox
* $C_{1},C_{2}$ : carrot

before any revelation

$$
P\{{\rm pick}=F\}=1/3 ,\qquad P\{{\rm pick}=C\}=2/3 .
$$

Let $R$ be the hole that is opened by the god and let $U$ be the other
closed hole.  The god is assumed to be able to find a carrot to show you,
so that

* if ${\rm pick}=F$ the two other holes are $C,C$.  The god shows one
$C$ and $U=C$;
* if ${\rm pick}=C$ the two other holes are $F,C$.  The god is forced to
show the $C$ and $U=F$.

Hence on the event “a carrot is shown’’

$$
P\{{\rm pick}=F\mid R=C\}=P\{{\rm pick}=F\}=1/3,
\qquad 
P\{{\rm pick}=C\mid R=C\}=P\{{\rm pick}=C\}=2/3,
$$

so the revelation carries no information about the initial pick.  In
particular

* $P\{{\rm stick\;is\;carrot}\}=P\{{\rm pick}=C\}=2/3$,
  $P\{{\rm stick\;is\;fox}\}=1/3$;
* $P\{U\;{\rm is\;carrot}\}=P\{{\rm pick}=F\}=1/3$,
  $P\{U\;{\rm is\;fox}\}=2/3$.

So staying with the first hole you chose leaves you with the original
$2/3$ chance of a carrot and $1/3$ chance of a fox, whereas moving to the
only other closed hole gives you a carrot with probability $1/3$ and a
fox with probability $2/3$.  Staying is the safe play.

*Remark.*  If the god is taken to open one of the two remaining holes
at random and we are simply told that the hole he opened happens to
contain a carrot, then $P\{{\rm pick}=F\mid R=C\}=P\{{\rm pick}=C\mid
R=C\}=1/2$ and the two closed holes are symmetric, $P\{{\rm stick\;is\;
carrot}\}=P\{U\;{\rm is\;carrot}\}=1/2$.  In that random-reveal
interpretation sticking and swapping are equivalent.

Linda is 31 years old, single, outspoken, active in the feminist movement, and very bright. She majored in philosophy. As a student, she was deeply concerned with issues of discrimination and social justice, and participated in anti-nuclear demonstrations. Which is more probable? (1) Linda is a bank teller. (2) Linda is a bank teller and is active in the feminist movement.

A. (2) is more probable
B. both are equally probable
C. (1) is more probable
content:
The conjunction of two propositions can never be more probable than either
of the conjuncts taken on its own.

For any two events $A$ and $B$

$$P(A\wedge B)=P(A)P(B|A)\le P(A)$$

with equality iff $P(B|A)=1$.  In particular

$$P({\rm bank\;teller})\ge P({\rm bank\;teller}\wedge {\rm feminist})$$

so on purely logical grounds the single proposition ‘Linda is a bank
teller’ is at least as probable as the conjunction ‘Linda is a bank
teller and Linda is active in the feminist movement’.  This is the
conjunction fallacy that is normally demonstrated with the Linda
profile: the feminist profile is highly representative of the description
and therefore the conjunction is judged more representative, and hence
more probable, than the single category ‘bank teller’.

*Remark.*  Conditional on the description $D$ that is given in the
stem $P({\rm feminist}|D)=1$, so that in the conditional world
$P({\rm bank\;teller}\wedge{\rm feminist}|D)=P({\rm bank\;teller}|D)$.
The conjunction is therefore logically redundant once the description
is taken as given.  This is the usual formalisation of the equality
case $P(A\wedge B)=P(A)$.

Final Answer: C

year,

$$P_{n}=P_{n-1}+P_{n-2}\qquad n\ge 2$$

with $P_{0}=P_{1}=1$ for a newborn pair.  Hence

* $P_{0}=1$
* $P_{1}=1$

A customer comes into a hardware store and picks up a boxed appliance from a stack of four. The sales clerk interrupts: 'One of the appliances may be defective', and proceeds to open one of the other boxes and tests the product, finding that it is in flawless order. Which box should the customer take?

A. the box the clerk tested
B. it makes no difference
C. the box the customer already picked up
D. one of the two untested boxes the customer did not pick
expected: A. the box the clerk tested
content:
The three boxes that have not been opened are exchangeable once the
information that the box which has been opened is good is taken into
account.

Put $D$ for the (unknown) defective box and let $C$ be the box first
taken by the customer and $O$ the box that the clerk actually opens.
A priori

$$
{\mathbb P}\{D=i\}=1/4\qquad i=1,\dots ,4 .
$$

Condition on the event $E=\{O\;{\rm is\;good}\}$ which is the event that
is actually observed.  For a fixed $O\ne C$

$$
{\mathbb P}\{E\mid D=C\}=1 ,\qquad 
{\mathbb P}\{E\mid D=i\}=1\qquad i\ne C,O ,
$$

and ${\mathbb P}\{E\mid D=O\}=0$.  Hence, up to the normalising constant,

$$
{\mathbb P}\{D=i\mid E\}\propto {\mathbb P}\{D=i\}{\mathbb P}\{E\mid D=i\}
$$

is $1/4$ for every $i\ne O$ and $0$ for $i=O$.  In particular

$$
{\mathbb P}\{D=C\mid E\}={\mathbb P}\{D=U_{1}\mid E\}={\mathbb P}\{D=U_{2}\mid E\}
      =\frac{1/4}{3/4}=\frac13 ,
$$

where $U_{1},U_{2}$ are the two boxes that are neither $C$ nor $O$.
The box $O$ that has been opened and tested is known to be good.  The
three unopened boxes $C,U_{1},U_{2}$ are therefore a posteriori
equiprobable, $1/3$ defective and $2/3$ good.  In particular the
customer’s original choice is a posteriori no better and no worse than
either of the two other unopened boxes, so that, on the information
actually given, there is no advantage in moving away from the box he
has already picked.  The only box that can be discarded with certainty
is the one that has been opened and found flawless.

*Remark.*  This is the ignorant-host version of Monty Hall.  If, as in
the usual Monty Hall formulation, the clerk is assumed to know where
the defective item is and is constrained to open a good box different
from $C$, then ${\mathbb P}\{D=C\mid E\}=1/4$ and
${\mathbb P}\{D\in\{U_{1},U_{2}\}\mid E\}=3/4$.  A random switch to one
of the two still-closed boxes that the customer did not pick then gives
a $3/8$ chance of picking the defective item against $1/4$ by staying,
i.e. the usual “switch’’ advantage.  This is the $D$ option usually
quoted for the knowledgeable-host Monty Hall problem.

userMessage: How many pairs of twins do you need in a room for there to be at least a 50 % chance that two people have the same birthday? Answer with a number.
content:
With the usual 365-day year the $n$-birthday problem is

$$P_{n}({\rm no\;collision})=\frac{365}{365}\frac{364}{365}\cdots
\frac{365-n+1}{365}\;,$$

so that $P_{n}({\rm collision})=1-P_{n}({\rm no\;collision})$ first
exceeds $1/2$ for

$$n=23\;{\rm independent\;birthdays},$$

i.e. for $2n=46$ people in the ordinary problem.

If a birthday is identified with a twin pair the $k$ pairs bring only
$k$ independent birthdays to the room.  The event “two different pairs
have the same birthday’’ – i.e. the non-trivial collision of birthdays
in the room – is therefore the ordinary birthday problem with $k$
birthdays.  The first $k$ for which

$$1-\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\frac{365-i}{365}\ge \tfrac12$$

is $k=23$ independent birthdays, i.e. $23$ twin pairs, $46$ people in
all.  This is the usual $23$-person $50\%$ birthday threshold applied to
the $k$ distinct twin-pair birthdays.

*Remark.*  In the literal wording a single twin pair already contains
two people with the same birthday, so the trivial collision probability
is $1$ as soon as $k\ge1$.

The centre of mass of a rigid body that is pivoted about the standing foot
moves on an arc whose radius is about one half the radius of the swinging
foot.  For a small rotation the vertical displacements are in the ratio

mass required to lift the toe a distance $h$ is of order $h/2$.

For $h=0.50\;{\rm m}$ this is

$\Delta z_{CM}\approx h/2\approx0.25\;{\rm m}$

in the idealised rigid–rod limit.  In particular the toe itself has to be
lifted at least $h=0.50\;{\rm m}$ above the ground.

Final Answer: 0.25

In a storeroom there are exactly three places where crates can stand, called place 1, place 2 and place 3. Five equally sized crates A, B, C, D and E are stacked as follows: on place 1, crate B stands on the floor with D on top of it; on place 2, crate A stands on the floor with C on top of it; on place 3, crate E stands alone. One move consists of lifting the topmost crate of one place and putting it down on another place (on the floor if that place is empty, otherwise on top of the stack there). The crates are to end up in one single stack on place 3, in alphabetical order with A on the floor and E on top. What is the smallest number of moves needed? Answer with a number.

userMessage: Five colleagues need a meeting of exactly 50 minutes on Thursday.
